# Introduction This is a book created from markdown and executable code. This page also works as a **reference of common content elements**: copy any of the examples below into your own chapters and adapt them. See @knuth84 for additional discussion of literate programming. ## Learning objectives By the end of this lesson, learners will be able to: - Describe the structure of a Quarto lesson. - Add images, tables and code to a chapter. - Use callouts to highlight tips, warnings and activities. ## Text formatting You can write text in **bold**, *italics*, `inline code`, ~~strikethrough~~ and [hyperlinks](https://quarto.org). Footnotes are added like this.[^1] [^1]: Footnotes appear at the bottom of the page (or chapter, in the PDF). > Block quotes are useful for highlighting a quotation or a key message. ## Lists Bullet points: - First item - Second item - Nested item - Another nested item - Third item Numbered steps: 1. Open the project in VS Code. 2. Edit a `.qmd` file. 3. Run `quarto preview` to see your changes. Task list: - [x] Write the introduction - [ ] Add exercises - [ ] Review the content ## Images Add an image with a caption and a label, so that you can cross-reference it as @fig-cover. ![The cover image of this lesson template.](images/rrcam-logo.webp){#fig-cover width=60% fig-alt="Cover image of the lesson template"} Always add `fig-alt` alternative text to make images accessible to screen reader users. ## Tables | Element | Syntax | Use it for | |----------|------------------|-------------------------------| | Bold | `**text**` | Key terms | | Code | `` `code` `` | Commands and file names | | Link | `[text](url)` | External resources | : Common markdown syntax. {#tbl-syntax} @tbl-syntax summarises the markdown syntax used on this page. ## Code ### Executable Python code Code in a ```` ```{python} ```` block runs when the book is built, and its output appears below it: ::: {.cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd data = pd.read_csv("data/example.csv") data.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
species island bill_length_mm body_mass_g
0 Adelie Torgersen 39.1 3750
1 Adelie Torgersen 39.5 3800
2 Adelie Biscoe 37.8 3400
3 Adelie Dream 40.3 3250
4 Adelie Dream 36.7 3450
``` ::: ::: Use `#|` options at the top of a cell to control it. Here, `echo: true` shows the code and `label`/`fig-cap` turn the plot into a numbered figure, @fig-body-mass: ::: {.cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt means = data.groupby("species")["body_mass_g"].mean() fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5)) means.plot.bar(ax=ax, color="#4C72B0") ax.set_xlabel("Species") ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)") plt.xticks(rotation=0) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Average body mass by penguin species.](intro_files/figure-html/fig-body-mass-output-1.png){#fig-body-mass width=527 height=319 fig-alt='Bar chart of average body mass for Adelie, Chinstrap and Gentoo penguins.'} ::: ::: Other useful cell options: - `#| echo: false` hides the code and shows only the output. - `#| eval: false` shows the code without running it. ### Display-only code Use a plain code block (without braces) for code that should be shown but not run, such as terminal commands: ```bash pip install -r requirements.txt quarto preview ``` ::: {.callout-note} To build this book, you need Python with the packages listed in `requirements.txt`. Install them with `pip install -r requirements.txt`. ::: ## Equations Inline maths: $E = mc^2$. Display maths with a label, cross-referenced as @eq-mean: $$ \bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i $$ {#eq-mean} ## Callouts ::: {.callout-note} ## Note Use a note for extra information. ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Tip Use a tip for helpful advice or shortcuts. ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## Warning Use a warning for common mistakes to avoid. ::: ::: {.callout-important} ## Important Use this for information learners must not miss. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Click to expand Collapsible callouts are useful for hints and solutions. ::: ## Tabsets Tabsets are useful for showing the same task in different languages. The Python tab runs; the R tab is display-only, because a page can only use one kernel. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("Hello, world!") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Hello, world! ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r print("Hello, world!") ``` :::
